passage:
At the edge of a Punjab village, the pan of boiling cane juice bubbled and smelled sweet. Five-year-old Gurpreet stood beside it, staring. "Is the gur ready? Is it ready?" He hopped from foot to foot and leaned toward the edge.
"Hot, puttar!" said Nirmala aunty, who ran the crusher. "It needs to set." She handed him a stick. "Count the buffaloes on the path for me. And sing the tractor song."
Gurpreet counted seven buffaloes, sang twice, and chased a hen. When Nirmala aunty called him, a warm lump of gur was waiting on a leaf.

qa.q: How many buffaloes did Gurpreet count?
qa.a: Gurpreet counted seven buffaloes.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet want while he hopped beside the pan?
qa.a: He wanted the gur right away, and staring at the bubbling pan made the wait feel too long to bear.

qa.q: Why was giving Gurpreet a job a wise choice?
qa.a: Counting buffaloes and singing took his eyes off the pan and kept him safely away from the heat while the gur set.

qa.q: How might Nirmala aunty feel with a small child hopping so close to the pan?
qa.a: She may feel worried about the hot pan and also fond of him, which is why she quickly gives him something else to do.

grounding: Shows a young boy who cannot wait while watching the sweet cook but manages well when given counting and a song.

passage:
Monday: Arnab's history project was due on Friday. At nine he lay on his bed with his phone. "Tomorrow I'll be fresh," he told his sister Kalyani when she asked. "Tuesday me is way more serious." He watched videos until midnight.
Wednesday: Tuesday had gone the same way. Now he scrolled with a small knot in his stomach, the empty project file open on the laptop behind the phone. "Tomorrow, full focus," he muttered. Kalyani raised an eyebrow and said nothing.
Friday, 6 a.m.: Arnab sat at the dining table, eyes red, gluing pictures onto chart paper and scribbling captions. He handed it in half-finished. That evening he asked Kalyani to keep his phone until eight.

qa.q: When was Arnab's history project due?
qa.a: Arnab's history project was due on Friday.

qa.q: Why did 'Tuesday me is way more serious' feel true to Arnab on Monday night?
qa.a: Tonight he felt tired and the videos were easy, so he imagined a fresher, more serious self tomorrow who would happily do the hard part.

qa.q: What turning point does Arnab reach, and why might it help?
qa.a: He asks Kalyani to keep his phone until eight, which removes the scrolling at the moment he usually gives in instead of trusting tomorrow's mood.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when Arnab hands her the phone on Friday evening?
qa.a: She may feel quietly glad, having watched the week unfold without lecturing, and pleased he chose the fix himself.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy who keeps pushing work to a tomorrow when he expects to feel keener, until the deadline arrives.

passage:
Sit, Sonali. You say you'll study tomorrow? Then let your Mehak Nani tell you about your Pradeep Mama when he was fifteen.
Every night he told me, "Ma, tomorrow I'll wake at five and finish algebra. Tonight I'm too tired." Then he sat on the terrace turning the pages of film magazines till eleven. In the morning? "Tonight, Ma, I'll feel more like it."
He truly believed the Pradeep of tomorrow would be a different boy, stronger. I watched this for a month. Then the half-yearly results came, and he cried on this same step.
After that, he did one small page each night before the magazines. Just one.
Tomorrow is a nice place, beta, but nobody lives there.

qa.q: What did Pradeep read on the terrace at night?
qa.a: He turned the pages of film magazines till eleven.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep keep believing tomorrow would be better?
qa.a: Each night he felt too tired, and he pictured a stronger Pradeep who would wake at five, so putting it off felt sensible, not lazy.

qa.q: What choice finally changed things for Pradeep?
qa.a: Doing one small page each night before the magazines, a task so small that tonight's tired self could still manage it.

qa.q: Why might Mehak Nani tell this story to Sonali instead of just scolding?
qa.a: Nani hopes Sonali will see the same pattern in the story of a beloved uncle and feel understood rather than judged.

grounding: An elder recalls a teenage son who always promised to study the next day, trusting that he would feel more willing then.

passage:
Uday's maths test was on Thursday, and his cousin Pallavi, the only one at home who understood trigonometry, was leaving for her hostel on Wednesday morning.
"Sit with me tonight," she offered on Monday.
"Tomorrow," Uday said, thumb flicking through short videos. "I'll feel sharper tomorrow."
On Tuesday a power cut hit at seven. When the fans spun again at ten, Uday was still scrolling. "Tomorrow morning, early," he told her.
On Wednesday at six, Pallavi's bag was by the door and the auto was honking. Uday ran out with his notebook. "Just one sum?"
She laughed tiredly and worked one sum with him on the auto step.

qa.q: What happened on Tuesday at seven?
qa.a: A power cut hit at seven.

qa.q: What did Uday expect to feel 'tomorrow', and why did that seem believable to him?
qa.a: He expected to feel sharper, because tonight he was comfortable scrolling and assumed a future Uday would be more in the mood for trigonometry.

qa.q: At which point could Uday have made a better choice, and what?
qa.a: On Monday, when Pallavi offered, he could have put the phone away and sat with her for even half an hour, since her help had a clear end date.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel working one sum on the auto step?
qa.a: She seems tired and a bit exasperated, yet still kind enough to help in her last minute, perhaps wishing he had come on Monday.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy who keeps delaying study until a time he believes he will feel more ready, even as his help is about to leave.

passage:
Thursday, 9:40 pm
Day 18 of the 6:30 walk. I almost skipped it. The alarm rang, the bed was warm, and the project report is due Monday, so "health" felt like a problem for later.
Then my phone buzzed: Rafiq, already at the park gate with his flask. "Where are you? Not walking past those dogs alone." That's our deal: whoever skips buys the other's tea for a week. So I went.
After the walk I had my reward: twenty minutes with my novel and a hot masala chai before opening the laptop. Tiny, but it's something to enjoy now, not in ten years.
Amma called tonight and said I sound less tired. "My early-bird daughter," she said. 😊
Vinita

qa.q: What is the deal between Vinita and Rafiq?
qa.a: Whoever skips buys the other's tea for a week.

qa.q: Why was skipping the walk tempting for Vinita this morning?
qa.a: The bed was warm and the Monday report felt urgent, so health seemed like a problem for later compared with rest right now.

qa.q: Which part of Vinita's system helps most on hard mornings, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq's message from the park gate, because letting down a friend who is already waiting feels worse than leaving a warm bed.

qa.q: What is the walk deal like from Rafiq's side?
qa.a: Rafiq also gets company and a reason to show up, and seems to count on Vinita as much as she counts on him.

grounding: Shows a young woman who keeps a morning walk going through a pact with a friend and a small reward right after.

passage:
In the hill town of Kalimpong, Dolma taught at the government school and came home tired every evening, tempted to sit with her phone until dinner.
In June she made two changes. She wrote "walk, 5:30" on the calendar that hung by the door, right beside the electricity bill, so it stared at her. And she made a pact with Sahil, the maths teacher next door, who wanted to get fitter himself: they would walk the ridge road together three evenings a week. At the bend, the tea stall owner kept two cups ready for them.
Some days Dolma's legs dragged. But Sahil was always at the gate, and the steaming cup at the bend was hers the moment she arrived. By August the calendar was full of ticks.

qa.q: Where did Dolma write her walk time?
qa.a: On the calendar that hung by the door, right beside the electricity bill.

qa.q: Why was sitting with her phone so tempting for Dolma?
qa.a: After teaching all day she came home tired, and resting felt good right now while fitness felt far off.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who wants to copy Dolma's habit?
qa.a: Put the time where you will see it, find a partner who is waiting for you, and give yourself a small treat along the way, like the tea at the bend.

qa.q: How does the pact help Sahil too?
qa.a: Sahil wanted to get fitter himself, so having Dolma to walk with gives him the same push and company on tired days.

grounding: Shows a young woman who uses a visible schedule, a walking partner and an immediate reward to keep a health habit.

passage:
At 7:30 in the hostel dining hall, after a day of tests, football practice and a debate round, Mridul stood at the counter with his plate.
"Dal or kadhi? Rice or roti?" asked the cook.
Mridul stared. "I don't know. Anything."
"Pick one, beta, the line is long."
His eyes filled. "I don't KNOW!"
Sumit, the senior monitor, stepped in and said calmly, "Dal and rice, same as me. Sit here."
Mridul nodded, sat, and ate without a word. Later, when Sumit asked which shirt he wanted ironed for the morning, Mridul just pushed both across. "You choose."

qa.q: What had Mridul done during the day before dinner?
qa.a: He had a day of tests, football practice and a debate round.

qa.q: Why might such a small choice make Mridul's eyes fill?
qa.a: After a long day his mind felt used up, so even dal or kadhi felt like one decision too many.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that helped, and what could the hostel try?
qa.a: Sumit made the choice for him calmly; the hostel could let tired juniors pick meals and shirts in the morning.

qa.q: What might the cook think when Mridul shouts 'I don't KNOW!'?
qa.a: The cook may be surprised or think he is being rude, not seeing how tired he is after such a full day.

grounding: Shows a boy who, after a packed school day, cannot choose between simple options and breaks down over them.

passage:
I'm Ganga, and from our balcony I can see into the courtyard of Farhan's house next door. Most weekdays he comes home at six, after school and then tuition.
Yesterday his Ammi held up two T-shirts for today's school picnic, a blue one and a striped one. Farhan stared at them for a long time, then threw his bag down and shouted, "I don't care!" A minute later he was crying about which pencil box to take.
On Sunday mornings I've seen him choose a kite colour in seconds, laughing. So maybe it isn't about the shirts at all. Maybe by evening he's just used up. I don't know for sure. His Ammi put the blue one out and sat beside him quietly.

qa.q: Which two T-shirts did Farhan's Ammi hold up?
qa.a: A blue one and a striped one.

qa.q: Why might Farhan shout 'I don't care!' over a T-shirt?
qa.a: Farhan may feel exhausted and overwhelmed after school and tuition, so even an easy choice about a T-shirt feels like too much.

qa.q: How could Farhan's Ammi make evenings easier for him?
qa.a: She could choose small things like shirts and pencil boxes herself on weekdays, or ask him in the morning when he is fresh.

qa.q: Why is Ganga unsure what is going on inside Farhan?
qa.a: Ganga only watches from a balcony and sees the outbursts, not his thoughts, but notices he chooses happily on Sunday mornings.

grounding: A neighbour describes a child who chooses easily when fresh but falls apart over tiny choices on weekday evenings.

passage:
Monday evening: After school, swimming and homework, Vikas stood in front of the fridge. "Mango juice or milk?" asked his father, Deepak. Vikas slammed the door. "Why do I have to choose everything?" and stomped off.
Wednesday evening: Same hour, and the question was which story to read. Vikas lay face-down on the carpet and would not answer. At dinner, Deepak noticed he had taken the plainest sandwich without even looking at the others.
Saturday morning: Rested, Vikas planned his whole weekend in five minutes, cheerfully. That night Deepak made a new rule: on school evenings he would set out two options before Vikas got home, or simply decide himself.

qa.q: What did Deepak ask Vikas on Monday evening?
qa.a: He asked, "Mango juice or milk?"

qa.q: Why did Vikas feel so fed up on Monday evening?
qa.a: After school, swimming and homework he had no energy left for choosing, so even a drink felt like one question too many.

qa.q: Was Deepak's new rule a good turning point? Why?
qa.a: Yes, because it removes small evening choices when Vikas is worn out, while Saturday shows he can decide well when rested.

qa.q: What was it like for Deepak to watch the difference on Saturday?
qa.a: Seeing Vikas plan the weekend cheerfully likely showed Deepak that the evening outbursts came from tiredness, not a difficult child.

grounding: Shows over a week how a tired boy refuses or rushes small evening choices but decides easily when rested.
